item.title: Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving
item.description: arXiv:2610.24369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
item.dc:creator: Haoze Wu, Andr\'e Schidler, Armin Biere, Nina Narodytska

item.title: The Lattice of Coalition Logics between MCL and CL: Coatoms and Compact Meets
item.description: arXiv:2610.24466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a fixed finite set $N$ of at least two agents, we investigate the lattice $L_N$ of coalition logics between minimal coalition logic (MCL) and classical coalition logic (CL), with extensions required to be structural. This lattice is order-dual to an interval in the subvariety lattice of Boolean coalition algebras. The eight basic extensions obtained by imposing seriality, independence of agents, and determinism form a Boolean cube under inclusion, but not a sublattice of $L_N$. Our main results concern coatoms and compact meets. First, finite critical coalition algebras, realized as complex algebras of finite general concurrent games, yield three infinite families of pairwise distinct coatoms containing seriality, distinguished by failures of independence, determinism, or both. An explicit splitting characterizes the unique coatom omitting seriality. Second, the meet of two basic extensions is compact if and only if the extensions are comparable. For incomparable pairs, no axiomatization of the meet can use formulas of uniformly bounded modal depth, even with infinitely many axioms. Consequently, $L_N$ and three natural principal intervals are non-coherent algebraic lattices. These results reveal lattice-theoretic phenomena beyond the inclusion order of the eight basic extensions.
item.dc:creator: Shanxia Wang, Yuqiang Dou

item.title: Taming Cyclic Dependencies in Stabilization-Based String Constraint Solving
item.description: arXiv:2610.25197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Word equations with cyclic variable dependencies pose a challenge to SMT string solvers. In stabilization-based procedures, such dependencies can trigger repeated refinement of regular-language assignments without reaching stability. We present Z3-Noodler-C, an extension of Z3-Noodler, combining equality-aware stabilization with dedicated loop reasoning. We introduce equality predicates to retain relevant equations as single stability obligations, and extend stabilization with equality-aware substitution and adapted concatenation-eliminating refinement to expose cyclic dependencies as overlapping variable bindings. Dedicated loop reasoning rules then exploit the periodic structure of these bindings, avoiding certain infinite derivations. We evaluate Z3-Noodler-C against Z3-Noodler, cvc5 and OSTRICH2. On 64 systematically generated, syntactically simple instances involving cyclic dependencies and regular constraints, our solver solves all instances, compared with only 20 solved for the best baseline. On equation-oriented instances from SMT-LIB'25, Z3-Noodler-C achieves the highest coverage, solving 20 more instances than Z3-Noodler while maintaining competitive aggregate CPU time.
item.dc:creator: Siyi Wu, Bican Xia

item.title: Neutrosophic Graph Rewriting as a Computational Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.25432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graphs, which are made up of points connected by lines, are used to represent relationships between objects. They are useful for solving problems in computer science, logistics, biology, and other fields, including social networks and the internet. Neutrosophic graphs are graphs whose points and lines are characterized by membership, indeterminacy, and non-membership degrees. In the simplest case, only lines are characterized by these degrees. The process by which we transform one graph to another is called graph rewriting. It has been shown that graph rewriting can be described mathematically by pushouts, which are category-theoretic structures. It has also been shown that fuzzy graphs have this property, and here we prove that neutrosophic graph rewriting can be described by pushouts in a certain category. By providing a fuzzy version of category theory, it is possible to define fuzzy categorical structures and thus to define neutrosophic graph rewriting in a more suitable manner. Since graph rewriting is actually a model of computation, neutrosophic graphs are a neutrosophic model of computation. A hypergraph is a generalization of a conventional graph. It allows a single "hyperline" to connect many points, which is different from regular graph lines that only connect two points. Neutrosophic hypergraphs can be used to reformulate Wolfram's models, which are supposed to be a mathematical model of reality.
item.dc:creator: Apostolos Syropoulos, Basil Papadopoulos, Binod Kumar Sharma

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Robust Monitoring of Dense-Time Temporal Logic
item.description: arXiv:2610.25639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by the use of third-party testing, this paper presents a privacy-preserving implementation of the robustness monitoring of Signal Temporal Logic (STL). STL is a specification language for systems whose output traces have real-valued timestamps -- most prominently, cyber-physical systems. Its robust semantics, which assign real rather than binary truth values, are an essential ingredient of systems testing and runtime monitoring. In a number of system testing scenarios, the designer and the tester are separate parties. This testing-as-a-service model is common in software, avionics, and semiconductors, and is growing in importance in the red-teaming of machine learning models. In such a model, the designer seeks to preserve the privacy (or secrecy) of its design, while the tester seeks to preserve the privacy of its collateral, including the detailed specification suite. This paper presents a secure multi-party implementation of the robust semantics using arithmetic circuits. This implementation allows one party, which provides a secret trace, and a second party which provides a secret formula, to jointly compute the robustness without either party being able to learn the other party's secret input. We present a number of algorithmic modifications to the robustness computation to enable an efficient multi-party robustness computation. We also present new, semi-linear, robust semantics for STL that take advantage of the efficiencies of arithmetic circuits. The experimental results demonstrate that not only is this privacy-preserving monitor efficient on its own, but also that it can be used in a testing loop without affecting the speed at which bugs are found during robustness-guided system testing.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 26th Conference on Formal Methods in Computer-Aided Design - FMCAD 2026 (2026) 271-283
item.dc:creator: Charles Koll, Mike Rosulek, Houssam Abbas

item.title: Beyond Leaderboards: A Method for Application-Specific Capability Profiling of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.25659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public leaderboards rank large language models (LLMs) in general, but an engineer has to choose a model for a specific application, architecture and cost. This paper presents a method for application-specific capability profiling of LLMs and its realization as a containerized testbed. The method treats each application as a unit of extension: an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration agent, a documentation-grounded chatbot or an enterprise-support automation agent runs in its own container behind a small contract, brings its own dataset, evaluator and owned attributes, and is onboarded together with its dashboards. Measurements accumulate in a versioned, sparse metamodel of every model. The method separates the model under test from judges and agents, freezes and hashes plans, refuses to compare values from different contexts, diagnoses the instrument before the system, and applies a null-agent check and a noise rule whose operating characteristics are quantified by simulation. In the evaluated automation conditions, model choices produced larger differences on selected observable outcomes than framework choices, although the experimental design does not establish a general causal ranking of these factors. The experiments also show that instruction tuning is deployment-specific and that system-reported success can exceed independently observed success: of 216 migration units checked against a real Oracle database, 108 were demonstrably correct. These measurements establish application-specific observations, not a universal model ranking.
item.dc:creator: Oleg Grynets, Vasyl Lyashkevych, Andrii Salyk, Dmytro Koziuberda, Dmytro Kostetskyi, Oleh Kaskun, Olena Pochernina, Alona Seletska, Oleksii Ilchuk, Viktoriia Tsymbal, Daryna Tukalo, Bohdan Saukh, Ivan Fedorchuk, Hryhorii Petrenko

item.title: Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Robust Stochastic Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.26193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Formal methods provide a principal approach to obtaining safety guarantees for autonomous agents. Their key bottleneck is their reliance on a formal model (e.g., a Markov decision process) describing the agent-environment interaction. Learning or crafting the model is an error-prone process, which undermines the guarantees offered by formal methods. Robust models account for modelling uncertainty, but may still fail to capture the true environment. This issue can be addressed through \emph{runtime model monitoring}, which aims to raise an alarm when a likely model-environment discrepancy is detected, while keeping the probability of false alarm bounded. Existing approaches impose various assumptions and do not clearly explain the rationale behind their design choices, leaving the broader design space for these monitors somewhat opaque. In this paper, we formalise the design space of monitors for robust stochastic models through the lens of \emph{parameterised sequential betting} algorithms, highlighting the importance of \emph{observation feature} design (choosing what information about the history the monitor uses) and \emph{bet design} (how rich a family of betting rules the monitor can represent). We show that our framework generalizes the existing approaches, and we use its formalization to propose a new \emph{mixture of linear monitors (ML)} design. We prove that these ML monitors achieve an asymptotically optimal detection time within the class of linear monitors, making them a principled choice for our monitoring problem. Our experiments confirm that ML monitors significantly reduce detection times compared to existing monitors and can effectively exploit more complex observation features.
item.dc:creator: Martin Kure\v{c}ka, Roman Andriushchenko, Milan \v{C}e\v{s}ka, Nicola Paoletti, Petr Novotn\'y

item.title: R\'ozsa: Certified Equational Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.26467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does one equation imply another? Stage 2 of the SAIR Mathematics Distillation Challenge required teams to submit solvers to answer this question for sets equipped with a binary operation. For these sets, associativity, commutativity, or any other algebraic property was not assumed. Each answer required a proof or counterexample that could be verified by Lean. Programs also had to respect fixed resource limits. We present R\'ozsa, a Python solver that searches for both kinds of evidence. It begins with simple tests and considers more extensive searches when those fail. To find a proof, it applies a given equation and derives any further equations as needed, keeping a record of each step. To find a counterexample, it searches for operations on finite sets. It also tests one fixed infinite model. The given equation must hold for every assignment, while the target equation must fail for at least one. In either case, R\'ozsa turns the evidence into a Lean certificate. The submitted solver solved 199/200 problems (99.5%) in the official main evaluation getting the 6th overall position. Additional tests show that the solver can prove many implications linked by long chains of known results, but has limited success with infinite counterexamples. We explain the search methods, how they fit together, and what the unsolved cases reveal about their limits.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Kissas

item.title: VoxLogicA2: A Spatial Model Checker for Neuro-symbolic Medical Imaging (extended version)
item.description: arXiv:2610.26626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the tool VoxLogicA2, a spatial model checker aimed at Computer Vision, with applications in high-resolution 2D and 3D medical imaging. The new version of the tool combines logical primitives, non-logical primitives, and training and prediction primitives of state-of-the-art neural networks, freely interleaved with the symbolic tool functionality. The primary application field is neuro-symbolic medical image analysis. VoxLogicA2 is a fast, parallelising spatial model checker with a declarative domain-specific language, capable of describing both the learning procedures and the spatial logic procedures of an analysis in one program. We validate our approach by verifying its improved efficiency, and by using the new constructs of the language to describe case studies of previous work, which were based on Python, with a specification that uses VoxLogicA2 only
item.dc:creator: Gina Belmonte, Laura Bussi, Vincenzo Ciancia, Mieke Massink

item.title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.24051v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
item.dc:creator: Savitha Sam Abraham, Marjan Alirezaie, Hossein Rahnama

item.title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
item.description: arXiv:2610.24690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.
item.dc:creator: Ali Ansari, Farhana Ferdousi Liza

item.title: A sound pure type system with ranks as sorts and Type-in-Type
item.description: arXiv:2610.25085v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a dependently typed pure type system that contains a circular axiom $s : s$ for a certain sort $s$ and is nonetheless strongly normalizing. Girard's paradox is avoided because our sorts are not closed under a $\Pi$-former: function types are placed in sorts according to their rank. Turns out that this system has a unique set of characteristics: it has similar normalization behaviour as STLC (so complexity of normalization is TOWER-complete) while at the same time allowing non-uniform representation of arbitrary elementary recursive functions; furthermore, it has a nontrivial set-theoretical model in ZF+GCH and allows to carry out nontrivial proof developments. Base normalization proof is surprisingly simple (modulo general metatheoretical properties of pure type systems) and has been fully formalized in vanilla Rocq (formerly Coq) without additional axioms.
item.dc:creator: Pavel Sokolov, Alexander Kuklev

item.title: Studying proof data with proof theory: the case of AI-generated mathematics
item.description: arXiv:2610.25357v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: I present a method for analyzing large collections of formally verified mathematical proofs (e.g. OpenAI's) grounded in some historical and philosophical musings on mathematics in the age of AI. Many of the quantities involved, such as the size of a proof term or the number of redundant steps, are already computed by work on improving automated provers, where they serve as targets. My aim is to turn them into measurements of proofs themselves: compared against a reference library and against each proof's own cut-free form, checked against theorems they must obey, and controlled for how the proofs were compiled. With these instruments, I measure how (much) machine-generated mathematics diverges from human mathematics, and find that AI-written formal proofs realize far less of the logical compression available to them than human mathematicians do (31% against 73% in mathlib, and 55% against 86% on proofs that call no automation). These figures are broadly in line with reports from those who build provers and proof-improvement tools that AI-written proofs are often longer than they need to be.
item.dc:creator: Safal Raman Aryal

item.title: Formalization of R\'{e}nyi Differential Privacy in Isabelle/HOL (Draft version)
item.description: arXiv:2610.25636v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a gold-standard definition of privacy designed to evaluate the privacy guarantee of databases. R\'{e}nyi differential privacy (RDP) is an important variant of DP that gives tight evaluations of machine learning algorithms. These formulations are easy to understand, but evaluating privacy for actual databases is complicated. Even a small change in the database can break its privacy, and evaluations of DP and RDP themselves are complicated. In particular, RDP evaluations in recent studies have become much harder. Therefore, formal verification of them has been studied for over a decade. In this paper, we propose an Isabelle/HOL library for formalizing R\'{e}nyi differential privacy in a general setting. We first formalize RDP for continuous distributions. As a technical basis, we formalize several properties of convex functions and $f$-divergences for nonnegative convex functions. We formalize basic properties of RDP, conversion laws from RDP to DP, the moment accountants in DP, and the Gaussian mechanism and its RDP. Finally, we discuss the stochastic gradient descent mechanism with Gaussian noise and formalize a rough evaluation of its RDP and DP.
item.dc:creator: Tetsuya Sato

item.title: On Counting Graphs for Modal Logic with Counting
item.description: arXiv:2610.26187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study the theoretical computational complexity of counting trees and graphs that are classified positively by a graph neural networks, or said equivalently that satisfy a given formula of modal logic with counting. We also study convergence.
item.dc:creator: Avijeet Ghosh, Fran\c{c}ois Schwarzentruber

item.title: A Type System for Communication-Safe Hardware Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.26599v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hardware components communicate through clock-cycle-sensitive protocols. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), however, provide limited support for expressing these protocols or for checking that independently developed components agree on them. When components disagree, the composed design can perform unsynchronized exchanges or stop making progress. We call these failures communication-safety violations. Communication safety is therefore a global property, determined by interactions between multiple components. This makes it difficult to check modularly. This paper presents Pact, a typed extension of Anvil for modular verification of communication safety in synchronous hardware. Pact types describe message-passing, control-flow, and clock-cycle behaviour. Each component is checked against its type. Compatible types then guarantee that the components compose into a communication-safe system. Pact also supports incremental design. It can check a subsystem before the full system context is available. The check produces a summary type that captures the communication behaviour left for future compositions. To reduce annotation burden, Pact infers types by abstracting payload values while preserving communication, timing, control, and fairness. These inferred types are optimal for the checker: whenever some checker-accepted types can prove compatibility, the inferred types can prove it as well. Type inference and type checking are decidable, and compatibility is decided by a sound and complete algorithm. We implement Pact by extending the Anvil compiler and evaluate it along four dimensions: detecting communication errors during incremental design, expressiveness on ten clock-cycle-accurate translations of open-source hardware IPs, compatibility-checking time, and generated hardware overhead. Pact expresses realistic protocols and verifies all ten benchmarks in reasonable time.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Ranjan Jha, Jason Zhijingcheng Yu, Umang Mathur, Prateek Saxena

item.title: Terminal Coalgebras in Countably Many Steps
item.description: arXiv:2303.11071v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a collection of results that imply that an endofunctor on a category has a terminal coalgebra obtainable as a countable limit of its terminal-coalgebra chain. This holds for finitary endofunctors on locally finitely presentable categories under conditions on both the functor and the category. We adapt finiteness arguments that were originally advanced by Worrell concerning terminal coalgebras for finitary set functors. Examples include the categories of sets, posets, vector spaces, graphs, nominal sets, and presheaves on finite sets. Worrell also described, without proof, the terminal-coalgebra chain of the finite power-set functor. We provide a detailed proof following his ideas. We then turn to polynomial endofunctors on the categories of Hausdorff topological spaces and metric spaces. The Vietoris space of compact subsets yields an endofunctor $\mathscr{V}$ on the category of Hausdorff spaces. Vietoris polynomial endofunctors are built from $ \mathscr{V}$, the identity and constant functors by forming products, coproducts and compositions. Their terminal coalgebras are obtained in $\omega$ steps. We then turn to the class of Hausdorff polynomial functors on the category of metric spaces, which is analogous but uses in lieu of $\mathscr{V}$ the Hausdorff functor $\mathcal{H}$. We prove they have terminal coalgebras obtained in $\omega + \omega$ steps. Finally, we show that every finitary endofunctor on the category of vector spaces over a fixed field again has a terminal coalgebra obtained in $\omega+\omega$ steps.
item.dc:creator: Ji\v{r}\'i Ad\'amek, Stefan Milius, Lawrence S. Moss

item.title: A Common Ancestor of PDL, Conjunctive Queries, and Unary Negation First-order Logic
item.description:
arXiv:2501.11641v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce and study UCPDL+, a family of expressive logics rooted in Propositional Dynamic Logic (PDL) with converse (CPDL) and universal modality (UCPDL). In terms of expressive power, UCPDL+ strictly contains PDL extended with intersection and converse (a.k.a. ICPDL), as well as Conjunctive Queries (CQ), Conjunctive Regular Path Queries (CRPQ), or some known extensions thereof (Regular Queries and CQPDL). Further, it is equivalent to the extension of the unary-negation fragment of first-order logic (UNFO) with unary transitive closure, denoted by UNTC, which in turn strictly contains a previously studied extension of UNFO with regular expressions known as UNFO$^{reg}$.
We investigate the expressive power, indistinguishability via bisimulations, satisfiability, and model checking for UCPDL+ and CPDL+. We argue that natural subclasses of CPDL+ can be defined in terms of the tree-width of the underlying graphs of the formulas. We show that the class of CPDL+ formulas of tree-width 2 is equivalent to ICPDL, and that it also coincides with CPDL+ formulas of tree-width 1. However, beyond tree-width 2, incrementing the tree-width strictly increases the expressive power. We characterize the expressive power for every class of fixed tree-width formulas in terms of a bisimulation game with pebbles. Based on this characterization, we show that CPDL+ has a tree-like model property. We prove that the satisfiability problem for UCPDL+ is decidable in 2ExpTime, coinciding with the complexity of ICPDL. As a consequence, the satisfiability problem for UNTC is shown to be 2ExpTime-complete as well. We also exhibit classes for which satisfiability is reduced to ExpTime.
item.dc:creator: Diego Figueira, Santiago Figueira

item.title: Property Directed Reachability with Extended Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2505.18998v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Property Directed Reachability (\textsc{Pdr}), also known as IC3, is a state-of-the-art model checking algorithm widely used for verifying safety properties. While \textsc{Pdr} is effective in finding inductive invariants, its underlying proof system, Resolution, limits its ability to construct short proofs for certain verification problems. This paper introduces \textsc{PdrER}, a novel generalization of \textsc{Pdr} that uses Extended Resolution (ER), a proof system exponentially stronger than Resolution, when constructing a proof of correctness. \PdrEV leverages ER to construct shorter bounded proofs of correctness, enabling it to discover more compact inductive invariants. While \PdrEV is based on \textsc{Pdr}, it includes algorithmic enhancements that had to be made in order to efficiently use ER in the context of model checking. We implemented \textsc{PdrER} in a new open-source verification framework and evaluated it on the Hardware Model Checking Competition benchmarks from 2019, 2020 and 2024. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that \textsc{PdrER} outperforms \textsc{Pdr}, solving more instances in less time and uniquely solving problems that \textsc{Pdr} cannot solve within a given time limit. We argue that this paper represents a significant step toward making strong proof systems practically usable in model checking.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Luka, Yakir Vizel

item.title: Forall-Exists Relational Verification by Filtering to Forall-Forall
item.description: arXiv:2509.04777v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Relational verification encompasses reasoning about data abstraction, security and privacy, secure compilation, and functional specification of tensor programs, among others. Several relational logics and tools support compositional reasoning about $\forall\forall$ (2-safety) properties and, generally, $k$-safety properties. In contrast, few logics and tools exist for reasoning about $\forall\exists$ properties which are critical in the presence of nondeterminism. This paper's primary contribution is a technique for verifying a $\forall\exists$ judgment by way of a novel transformation. The filter-adequacy transformation adds assertions to a product program in such a way that the desired $\forall\exists$ property (of a pair of underlying unary programs) is implied by a $\forall\forall$ property of the transformed product. The paper develops bicoms, a form of product programs that facilitates expressing good alignments and caters for direct translation of $\forall\forall$ properties to unary correctness; proves that successful $\forall\forall$ verification of a transformed bicom implies the $\forall\exists$ spec for its underlying unary commands; and evaluates the technique using a prototype auto-active relational verifier. The technique enables users to work with ordinary assertions and assumptions, and a standard assertion language, so that existing $\forall\forall$ and unary verification tools can be used for $\forall\exists$.
item.dc:creator: Ramana Nagasamudram, Anindya Banerjee, David A. Naumann

item.title: A Dichotomy Theorem for Homomorphism Problems on Automatic Structures
item.description: arXiv:2602.18238v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The field of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) studies homomorphism problems between relational structures where the target structure is fixed. Classifying the complexity of these problems has been a central quest of the field, notably when both sides are finite structures. In this paper, we study the generalization where the input is an automatic structure---potentially infinite, but describable by finite automata. We prove a striking dichotomy: homomorphism problems over automatic structures are either decidable in non-deterministic logarithmic space (NL), or undecidable. We show that structures for which the problem is decidable are exactly those with finite duality, which is a classical property of target structures asserting that the existence of a homomorphism into them can be characterized by the absence of a finite set of obstructions in the source structure. Notably, this property precisely characterizes target structures whose homomorphism problem is definable in first-order logic, which is well-known to be decidable over automatic structures. We also consider a natural variant of the problem. While automatic structures are finitely describable, homomorphisms from them into finite structures need not be. This leads to the notion of "regular homomorphism", where the homomorphism itself must be describable by finite automata. Remarkably, we prove that this variant exhibits the same dichotomy, with the same characterization for decidability.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Cuvelier, R\'emi Morvan

item.title: Synthetic Differential Geometry in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2603.17457v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This article is about the formalization of synthetic differential geometry with the Lean proof assistant and the mathematical library mathlib. The main result we prove and formalize is a Taylor theorem for functions of several variables, where the series expansion is around an infinitesimal neighborhood. Most of our proofs are in fact new. Our investigations highlight the possibility of using mathlib to do constructive mathematics.
item.dc:creator: Riccardo Brasca (IMJ-PRG), Gabriella Clemente (IRIF)

item.title: Formalizing a Many-Sorted Hybrid Polyadic Modal Logic in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2606.27041v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a Lean formalization of a general hybrid modal logic with many-sorted signatures and polyadic modal operators. The system borrows ideas from both algebraic specification and dynamic logics, and is designed to serve as a uniform axiomatic foundation for specifying and verifying programming languages and security protocols. We expose a DSL for users to define languages and protocols as many-sorted signatures, specify the relevant domain-specific axioms, and reason about program executions or protocol runs. We provide a machine-checked proof of its soundness theorem and showcase the framework's versatility through several applications: an imperative programming language for code verification, a BAN logic and an epistemic logic used for security protocols, and the modal system S5. We have designed our formalization to be intrinsically sorted, that is, well-sorted formulas in the base language are well-typed terms in Lean. Thanks to intrinsic sorting, all domain specific applications can be easily embedded in our framework via the DSL, at no additional syntactic overhead required for the user to prove. All code presented in this paper is openly accessible in the following repository: https://github.com/alexoltean61/msphml-lean
item.dc:creator: Alexandru Oltean, Bogdan Macovei, Ioana Leu\c{s}tean

item.title: Reasoning about Continuous-Variable Quantum Systems
item.description: arXiv:2607.23137v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum computing (CVQC) is a computing paradigm in which measurements yield values over a continuous domain. CVQC is both a convenient computational framework for modeling physical quantum systems, and a good abstraction for hardware platforms based on quantum optics. Yet, the semantic foundations of CVQC remain underdeveloped. To address this gap, we develop a formal semantics for a core CV quantum programming language, and sound verification methods for program correctness. A main contribution of this work is to isolate a well-behaved quantitative predicate domain that achieves sufficient expressiveness to accommodate unbounded values as they arise in the infinite-dimensional, continuous setting. Specifically, we choose closed positive quadratic forms as semantic predicates, representing finite expectations, domains of finiteness, and infinite penalties in one ordered object. We validate our choice by establishing that our semantic predicates satisfy desirable closure properties including the definition of weakest preconditions. We validate our design with two case studies, including an example based on the celebrated GKP error-correcting code, for which we establish a second moment bound.
item.dc:creator: Tianshi Yu, Gilles Barthe, Minbo Gao, Mingsheng Ying, Li Zhou

item.title: The Myhill isomorphism theorem does not generalize much
item.description: arXiv:2507.05028v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Myhill isomorphism is a variant of the Cantor-Bernstein theorem. It states that, from two injections that reduce two subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ to one another, there exists a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that preserves them. This theorem can be proven constructively. We investigate to which extent the theorem can be extended to infinite sets other than $\mathbb{N}$. We show that, assuming Markov's principle, the theorem can be extended to the conatural numbers $\mathbb{N}_{\infty}$ provided that we only require that bicomplemented sets are preserved by the bijection. This restriction is essential. Otherwise, the picture is overall negative: among other things, it is impossible to extend that result to either $2 \times \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N} + \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N}_{\infty}^2$, $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$.
item.dc:creator: C\'ecilia Pradic

item.title: Cyclic Graphs and Memoization in Pure $\lambda$-Calculus
item.description: arXiv:2606.22908v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Purely functional programming makes immutability and non-strict evaluation its defaults; we push further, making interning and memoization the defaults of computation. In prior operational semantics for the pure $\lambda$-calculus, representing and transforming cyclic and infinite data requires an added recursion construct, a $\texttt{letrec}$, a $\mu$-binder, or a built-in $Y$ for graph reduction, and sharing the repeated work of a memoized or dynamic-programming function requires an impure cache. We show that no extension is needed. We apply tabling, the standard method for solving a least-fixpoint equation, to weak-head reduction; this defines a new operational semantics for the pure $\lambda$-calculus that keeps each term's standard lazy meaning. A term that reaches finitely many distinct states, each solved in finitely many steps, comes out as a finite graph, possibly cyclic; the calculus stays pure, and the graph is faithful and independent of reduction order. We implemented this operational semantics as a $\lambda$-calculus interpreter. It does dynamic programming automatically, sharing repeated subproblems with no memoization table. It creates and transforms cyclic graphs with no added recursion construct. And it decides in finite time that some terms have no weak head normal form, returning $\bot$ for $\Omega$. What the evaluator returns is a graph, so the $\lambda$-calculus becomes a DSL for graph computation: the memo table of dynamic programming, the transposition table of game search, and the derived-fact table of Datalog reachability and points-to analysis are all tabling on state identity, and none of them is written by hand. Compilation is one more such problem: we write a bootstrap compiler that compiles its own source, all as a pure $\lambda$-term.
item.dc:creator: Bo Yang

item.title: MathAdv: What Theorem Provers Know, Reason, Formalize, and Generalize
item.description: arXiv:2608.25449v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Formal theorem proving enables machine-verifiable evaluation of mathematical reasoning, yet existing benchmarks often emphasize aggregate proof accuracy, concentrate on a narrow range of mathematics, and provide limited evidence of robustness to equivalent reformulations. We introduce MathAdv, a diagnostic benchmark spanning 13 domains across undergraduate- and graduate-level mathematics. Alongside Lean 4 theorem proving, MathAdv provides up to three auxiliary tasks: multiple-choice questions that probe mathematical knowledge, fill-in-the-blank problems that isolate informal reasoning, and expert-crafted transformations that test robustness to problem presentation. Our evaluation of contemporary theorem provers yields four findings: formalization remains a major bottleneck; performance varies substantially across mathematical domains; natural-language guidance helps general-purpose LLMs but can hinder proof-specialized models; and mathematically equivalent reformulations expose substantial robustness limitations. Together, these results show how component-wise evaluation can reveal model capabilities and failure modes that aggregate theorem-proving accuracy obscures. The dataset and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/margotyjx/MathAdv.git.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxin Yuan, Udari Madhushani Sehwag, Connor Martinez Lockhart, Xiaoyu Liu, Shayan Shabihi, Jiaqi Wang, Chenghao Deng, Xiayimei Han, Vlassis Mastrantonis, Dmitrii Gudin, Shaopeng Zhu, Abdirisak Mohamed, Bilal Aytekin, Jiewen Lang, Zezheng Song, Furong Huang

item.title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22287v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.
item.dc:creator: Omar Adalat, Edwin Hamel-De le Court, Francesco Belardinelli
